title: Shit.
body:
Wednesday two weeks ago I got a call at 7am from Dad back in NZ, calls at this time are never good. And it wasn't. Dad's got pancreatic cancer. Shit. I kept saying that back to him about 10 times in different tones.

My mind flashed back to my brief time working in oncology in Wellington and the people coming in for a Whipple's (a massive 12 hour surgery) just to get a bit more time. But unfortunately, Dad's is a bit beyond that point and his cancer is inoperable, therefore not curable. After he saw the surgeon he very stoically said… "These are just the cards I've been dealt"

It's been a whirlwind two weeks involving countless appointments, scans, tough decisions and harder conversations. Working through the finer details of how you might like to die and everything after is a brutally confronting exercise. But we got through all of this in the space of a few days with the goal of preparing for the worst, and hoping for the best.

He's had an astounding number of people reach out to him, and he doesn't want anyone to be left out of the loop. So I'm going to write these up for whoever wants to keep tabs on what's happened, happening next and maybe how they might be able to help from time to time.

So, where we're at: he has pancreatic adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastases.

The plan is to (ideally) start chemo Wednesday next week. He's got a biopsy on Monday and that'll work out if he's a candidate for drug trials. These will hopefully give him a bit more time and if all goes well it'll be 4+ years, worst case it might be 5 months. The odds seem to get better with each new appointment and Dad's got a lot on his side. And there's plenty of people that have gotten out of worse scenarios! (Most recent update from today, the cancer hasn't grown in two weeks! Great news!!)

There's also a challenge around his stomach being affected which has had some radiation this week. And then a lot of trial and error working out how much insulin he needs as his pancreas can't make any. (Update — required a short stay in hospital as sugars were beyond what the monitor could read for about 3 days)

It feels like we've got as much in place, as quickly as we possibly could. We're eternally grateful for all of the amazing people that got him there so quickly and all of the offers for help. Thanks so so much.

I'm on my way back to London after 10 days at home in Christchurch and grateful that I just managed to get back in time for Dad's birthday on the 26th. It's been a really nice time together as a family, playing golf, watching rugby and doing the little things Dad enjoys in his day.

The whole experience seems to have given his humour an extended license and he's been gloating how he's being let off the hook for falling asleep with a glass of wine in his hand. But after everything, he's still putting everyone first. All classic Terry traits.

Nick
